title: Explaining Events & Ideas
keyIdea: To explain an event from a non-fiction text, say what happened and why. Causes come before the event and help make it happen; effects come after, because of it; dates and names are details, not reasons. Back each cause with the sentence that says it, use because, so and as a result to show the reason (then only shows the order), and notice chains where one effect becomes the cause of the next thing. A process is explained the same way: each step, and the reason it is needed.
familyTip: After a news story or a film, ask two questions: what happened, and why? Ask for two causes and one effect. Then ask: how do you know? Point to the line or the moment that shows it. Listen out for 'and then', and ask whether it should be 'because' or 'so'.

visual.caption: Why did the river flood the town, and what did it lead to? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

Shops put sandbags at the door

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort causes and effects of the Great Fire, prove claims with a sentence, pick because or so, order a firebreak, build a chain.

kid: To explain an event, say what happened and why. What happened is the event. Why it happened are the causes. What it led to are the effects.

A cause comes first and helps make the event happen. In 1666 a fire began in a bakery in London. A dry summer, a strong wind and houses packed close made it spread. Those are causes. Then 13,200 houses burned. That is an effect.
Back up each cause with the text. Say which sentence tells you. Sentence 4 says a strong wind blew sparks from roof to roof. Now anyone can check it.
Use because and so to show a reason. Then just tells you the order. One thing can lead to the next, like links in a chain. The dry summer dried the houses, so sparks set roof after roof on fire.
adult: Ages 9 to 10. The US Common Core asks pupils in grade 4 to explain events, procedures and ideas in a historical, scientific or technical text, including what happened and why, based on specific information in the text (RI.4.3). Grade 5 adds the links between two or more events (RI.5.3). In England, KS2 reading asks pupils to retrieve and record information from non-fiction and explain what they understand.

A full explanation has three parts: the event, its causes and its effects, each tied to a sentence the reader can find. A process works the same way: each step plus the reason it is needed. Signal words help: because, so, as a result, therefore and this led to.

Common mistakes: treating order as cause (it came after, so it must be because of it); giving one cause when the text gives several; mixing up cause and effect; listing dates or names as if they were reasons; and making claims without pointing to the text. Be careful with 'and then': it shows order, not a reason.

In the lab your child sorts causes, effects and details for the Great Fire of London, taps the sentence that proves each claim, chooses because or so instead of then, orders the steps of a firebreak with a reason for each, and builds a chain where each effect causes the next link.

practice.prompt: The Great Fire of London was in 1666. How many years before {y} was that?
practice.hint: Take the year of the fire away from {y}.
practice.explain: {y} take away 1666 is {=y-1666}, so the fire was {=y-1666} years before {y}.

practice.prompt: Your explanation gives {n} causes. Each cause needs a because sentence and a sentence from the text to back it up. How many sentences is that?
practice.hint: Each cause needs 2 sentences: the reason and the proof.
practice.explain: {n} causes with 2 sentences each makes {=2*n} sentences.

practice.prompt: Which is a cause of the fire spreading?
practice.hint: A cause comes before the spread and helps make it happen.
practice.explain: The wind blew sparks from roof to roof, so it is a cause. Rebuilding came after (an effect), and the day is just a detail.

practice.prompt: Pick the best word: The houses were made of dry wood, ___ they burned quickly.
practice.hint: The dry wood comes first. Which word points on to what it led to?
practice.explain: So points from the cause (dry wood) to the effect (burning quickly). Because would flip them, and then only gives the order.

practice.prompt: Which sentence explains a step in a process?
choices: Houses were pulled down before the flames came, so the fire had nothing to burn
Many houses were made of wood
practice.hint: Look for the step and the reason for it.
practice.explain: It gives the step and why it works. The second gives the step with no reason, and the third is a fact, not a step.

pool.prompt: A text says: 'The river flooded because it rained for five days.' Which part is the cause?
pool.hint: Which part came first and made the other happen?
pool.explain: The rain came first and made the river flood, so the rain is the cause. The flood is the effect, and because is the signal word.

pool.prompt: The text goes on: 'As a result, the bridge was closed.' Which is an effect of the flood?
pool.hint: As a result points to what came after.
pool.explain: The bridge closed because of the flood, so it is an effect. The rain is a cause, and the width of the river is a detail.

pool.prompt: Mo writes: 'The fire started on a Sunday, so it spread.' What is wrong?
choices: The day did not make it spread; it only tells when
Nothing, it is a good explanation
pool.hint: Did the day of the week help the flames move?
pool.explain: Sunday is a detail. The wind, the dry wooden houses and the stores of oil and tar made it spread.

pool.prompt: Which claim is backed up by the text?
choices: The wind helped: sentence 4 says it blew sparks from roof to roof
The wind helped, I just know it
The wind helped, everyone says so
pool.hint: Which one could a reader check?
pool.explain: Naming the sentence lets anyone check it. Knowing it or everyone saying it is not proof from the text.

pool.prompt: Why was the fire hard to stop at first?
choices: The Lord Mayor would not let houses be pulled down
The bakery was on Pudding Lane
pool.hint: Look for what someone in charge did, or did not do, at the start.
pool.explain: Sentence 6 says the Lord Mayor would not let houses be pulled down, so no gaps were made early. The street name and the year are details.

pool.prompt: Which phrase tells you an effect is coming next?
pool.hint: Which phrase points on to what something led to?
pool.explain: As a result introduces an effect. Before that gives order in time, and once upon a time starts a story.

pool.prompt: A cause chain has {n} links in a row, joined by arrows. How many arrows join them?
pool.hint: Each arrow joins one link to the next. Count the gaps between links.
pool.explain: {n} links have {=n-1} gaps between them, so there are {=n-1} arrows, one for each cause leading to an effect.

pool.prompt: Making a firebreak takes 3 steps. A team makes {n} firebreaks. How many steps do they carry out in all?
The chain so far: dry summer, houses dry out, sparks set roofs alight. What comes next?
pool.hint: What did the burning roofs lead to?
pool.explain: Roof after roof on fire led to thousands of houses burning. The dry summer is the first link, not the next one.
